top_stories.title: Tech selloff: Alphabet, Intel lead mega-cap declines on AI spending fears
points: Alphabet lost roughly $500-530 billion in market cap in one session despite beating on search growth, as investors worried about AI eroding search ad monetization.
Intel shares plunged 28-29%, its worst trading day since 1974, erasing about $140 billion in value, even though its data-center/AI segment grew 78% year-on-year to $7.3 billion, beating estimates.

Analysts (Evercore ISI's Mark Mahaney) describe the rout as an 'expectations correction, not a fundamentals correction'—Amazon's AWS also beat estimates (40% growth to $45.9B) yet its stock sold off too.

Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta are each spending $100B-$200B annually on AI infrastructure (capex), pushing free cash flow negative and forcing bond sales (Microsoft $25B) and stock offerings (Meta $95B) to fund the buildout.

Oaktree's Howard Marks said the stumbles have deflated AI's 'halo of invincibility,' while Morgan Stanley's Michael Wilson told investors to prepare to add risk, framing the selloff as a possible buying opportunity.

Apple stands apart, keeping capex near $10B/year versus rivals' much larger spend, relying instead on third-party AI models and partners; new CEO John Ternus holds his first earnings call with hardware launches (touchscreen MacBooks, HomeView hub, foldable iPhone Duo) in focus.

unique_angles.point: Soaring memory chip costs (needed for AI hardware) are adding further pressure to already strained capex budgets across the industry.

Sector rotation accompanied the selloff: energy and consumer staples each gained over 10% in October while tech fell 8.2% and communication services dropped 9.9%; the equal-weight S&P 500 (an index weighting all 500 stocks equally rather than by size) beat the cap-weighted index by 5.8 points in October, the second-best such month since 1990.
SpaceX lost over $400 billion in market value in under a month, reflecting broader valuation pressure beyond public tech giants.
Morgan Stanley's Michael Wilson explicitly urged investors to 'get ready to add risk,' suggesting the dip may be a buying entry point rather than a sustained downturn.

top_stories.title: Binance suffers record-breaking crypto hack, sparking withdrawal rush
points: Binance, a major cryptocurrency exchange, suffered the largest crypto heist in history, with reported losses ranging from $3.6B to $6.4B depending on the source.
The exchange briefly suspended withdrawals but pledged to 'cover all losses,' stating user funds are safe.

Despite assurances, customers pulled a net $3.6-4.7 billion from the platform after withdrawals resumed, and Bitcoin-linked tokens like Ethereum and Binance's own BNB token fell in response (ether down 4% to $2,200, BNB down 5%).

The FBI attributed the theft to North Korean hackers, who are reportedly converting stolen funds into Ethereum and plan to launder them via DeFi (decentralized finance: peer-to-peer financial services built on blockchain) and instant-swap services, possibly aided by AI tools.

unique_angles.point: Framed alongside Fitch's downgrade of France's credit outlook, citing high borrowing costs and a widening budget deficit, as part of a broader day of risk-off headlines.
Clear Street's Owen Lau warned the industry lacks a regulatory framework to protect investors, and noted the crypto industry is pursuing legislation to align with banking-style standards.
Experts believe North Korean hackers have incorporated powerful AI tools into their operations, raising concern about more sophisticated future attacks.

top_stories.title: Oil prices fall ahead of key economic and geopolitical catalysts
points: Crude oil prices dropped sharply Monday morning, with traders citing both diplomatic de-escalation hopes between the U.S. and Iran and caution ahead of major economic data.
Reports (via Axios) say Trump told Israeli PM Netanyahu he wants to give diplomacy more time before any renewed strikes on Iran, easing some geopolitical risk.
Gulf Arab states reportedly fear that a new U.S.-Israeli strike on a better-prepared Iran could ignite a far more destructive regional war.
Falling oil is also read as a signal of investor expectations for slower economic growth, with Friday's jobs report seen as a potential catalyst for Fed policy direction.

unique_angles.point: Energy-sector volatility is framed as generally intensifying ahead of major data releases, with oil serving as a broad inflation and growth signal.
Oil's decline is directly tied to Trump's diplomatic messaging on Iran, providing a tailwind for stock futures in early trading.
Oil's slide is attributed specifically to hopes for U.S.-Iran negotiations amid a broader Monday market recovery from Friday's selloff.

top_stories.title: Big week ahead: Apple/Palantir earnings, midterm elections, and jobs report
points: Apple and Palantir report earnings today (Monday), with Apple's results closely watched given its distinct AI/capex strategy versus rivals.
U.S. midterm elections take place Tuesday, covering all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats plus major gubernatorial races, injecting political uncertainty into markets.

Friday's October nonfarm payrolls (jobs) report is seen as pivotal, with weak employment potentially easing pressure on the Fed to keep raising rates; CME FedWatch shows ~76% odds of a December rate hike.
Additional earnings expected throughout the week include AMD, Marathon Petroleum, Arm, McDonald's, Qualcomm, Uber, Toyota, and ConocoPhillips, alongside JOLTS, ADP, and services PMI data.

unique_angles.point: St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said another rate hike needs to happen soon, reinforcing hawkish signals despite market volatility.

Midterm results are expected to shape policy on AI, data centers, and cost of living; California's Proposition 40 wealth tax vote prompted Meta to issue new shares to protect Zuckerberg's voting control.
Noted that Intel shares kept falling in Monday premarket trading even as the broader market rebounded, highlighting company-specific weakness distinct from the overall recovery.

Friday's 1.8% drop was the worst single day since June.
More than 300 S&P 500 stocks still rose last week despite the index falling over 0.5%, indicating broad participation beyond mega-cap stocks and challenging narratives about market concentration.

sections.title: The Five-Month Stalemate
points: 1. S&P 500 closed Friday at 7,580.07, essentially matching May 29's 7,580.06 close—one penny of progress across five months despite significant intra-period volatility.
2. Index fell to 7,266 in June and peaked at 7,818 on October 6 before giving back all gains, with Friday's 1.8% drop marking worst day since June.
3. Equal-weight S&P 500 (an index that treats all 500 stocks equally rather than weighting by company size) rose 4.5% in same period, outperforming cap-weighted index by 5.8 points in October alone.

4. October's equal-weight outperformance was the second-best month against cap-weighted S&P 500 since 1990, with monthly swing from September exceeding 10 points—the largest reversal in either direction since 1990.

sections.title: Market Rotation and Sector Shifts
points: 1. Energy and consumer staples both gained more than 10% in October while tech fell 8.2% and communication services dropped 9.9%.

2. Equal-weight's October outperformance marks only the fourth instance since 1990 when it outperformed by five or more points in a single month (1999, 2000, 2002, 2009), with two of those instances following major market lows.
3. More than 300 S&P 500 stocks rose last week despite the index falling more than 0.5%, indicating broad participation outside mega-cap leaders.
4. The shift challenges media narratives about top-heavy market concentration from earlier in the year.

sections.title: Major Earnings and Corporate Moves

issues.subject: Morning Brief: Big Tech's sell-off wasn't about the actual fundamentals

headlines: Big Tech earnings miss triggered sell-off despite strong cloud growth—Alphabet, Amazon, and Intel posted bullish fundamentals but investors have become more demanding.
Binance suffered $6.3 billion crypto hack, the largest in history; exchange suspended withdrawals but promised to cover all losses.
Apple and Palantir report earnings Monday; midterm elections Tuesday will shape policy on AI, data centers, and cost of living.
SpaceX lost over $400 billion in market value in less than a month as valuation pressures mount.
US completes second-largest oil reserve release ever as energy markets remain volatile.

sections.title: Tech Stock Rout Was About Expectations, Not Fundamentals
points: Alphabet missed on revenue and profit; shares fell 13% despite search growth, as AI erodes search monetization (the primary way search engines make money from ads).
Amazon reported AWS (cloud and AI unit) revenue of $45.9 billion, up 40% and beating $44.8 billion estimates, yet overall stock sold off on double miss elsewhere.
Intel's data center and AI segment grew 78% year-on-year to $7.318 billion against estimates of $6.675 billion, but stock lost 28% on broader PC weakness.
Analyst Mark Mahaney (Evercore ISI) characterized the selloff as 'an expectations correction and not a fundamentals correction'—investors raised the bar after initial optimism.

sections.title: Binance Hack Threatens Confidence in Crypto Exchange Security
points: $6.3 billion in digital assets stolen late Thursday in what investigators call the biggest crypto hack ever; ether fell 4% to $2,200, and Binance's native token BNB dropped 5%.
Binance temporarily suspended customer withdrawals but stated it would 'cover all losses' and that 'user funds are safe.'
Crypto industry pursuing new legislation to shift regulatory framework toward banking standards; hack raises immediate questions about trust and protection mechanisms.
Clear Street managing director Owen Lau warned: 'We need a good regulatory framework to really protect the industry and also give confidence to investors. Right now, we don't have it.'

sections.title: Midterm Election Outcomes Will Shape Tech Policy and Labor Markets
points: 470 elections occurring this week: all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats, plus major gubernatorial races expected to influence data center development policy.

Key races include Ohio Senate (Sherrod Brown vs. Jon Husted) and Texas gubernatorial (Greg Abbott vs. Gina Hinojosa); California Proposition 40 wealth tax vote prompted Meta to issue new shares to protect Zuckerberg's voting control.
Election outcomes will influence cost of living and AI policy trajectories, both major issues affecting future labor market shifts.
Friday nonfarm payrolls report will provide first major labor market snapshot post-election, serving as capstone to the week's political and economic events.

Wednesday-Thursday: Arm, McDonald's, Qualcomm, Uber, Toyota, and ConocoPhillips among major earnings; ADP employment and services PMI data.
